applied_rule_restatement.scoring_procedure: C = the published total package count of the single qualifying index selected by index_selection_rule (largest self-published total among qualifying indexes). Bands: C>=100000 -> 100 'Very large library population'; 10000<=C<100000 -> 80 'Large'; 1000<=C<10000 -> 60 'Moderate'; 100<=C<1000 -> 40 'Small'; 1<=C<100 -> 20 'Nascent'; C=0 -> 0 'No qualifying index'.
applied_rule_restatement.qualification_clauses: (i) referenced by a member of the language's official_project_set in official documentation; (ii) default remote of a package manager that the language's official documentation names; (iii) published or maintained by a maintainer of an implementation listed in that language's frozen major_implementations.
applied_rule_restatement.precondition_test_applied_identically_to: The rubric's qualification precondition is 'distributes libraries for that language'. Applied uniformly as: the index's published population must be obtainable as libraries by that language's normal build toolchain, evidenced either by (a) the index's own self-description naming the language, or (b) the language's official documentation directing users of that language to obtain dependencies from that index. This test excluded general-purpose OS/software package archives (Homebrew, Debian/apt) for C++ and excluded NuGet for C++ (self-describes as the package manager for .NET; no official C++ documentation root in official_project_table directs C++ users to it). It admitted CocoaPods for Swift (self-describes as 'a dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C Cocoa projects'), Maven Central for Kotlin and npm for TypeScript (official documentation of each directs users there). The same test was written down before the ten selections were fixed and applied to every language.
applied_rule_restatement.index_totals_not_language_filtered: The rubric measures 'the total published package count' of the selected index, not a language-filtered subset. This is why Java and Kotlin both take Maven Central's total, TypeScript takes npm's total, C++ takes vcpkg's total and Swift takes CocoaPods' total.

cross_language_consistency_note: The metric is a single measured quantity with frozen bands, so consistency was enforced on the three steps that produce that quantity rather than on prose. (1) Qualification: every index was tested against the same three clauses, and the satisfied clause is recorded per language - (i) for Python, Kotlin, Swift and TypeScript, (ii) for Rust, Java and Go, (iii) for C++. Quidra and Zig were tested against the identical clauses and failed all three, which is why they take the level-0 band rather than an N/A. (2) The 'distributes libraries for that language' precondition was written down as one test and applied to all ten before the selections were fixed; it is what excludes NuGet, Homebrew and Debian for C++ while admitting CocoaPods for Swift, Maven Central for Kotlin and npm for TypeScript, and it is stated in applied_rule_restatement so an auditor can re-run it. (3) Counts are the index's own published totals in nine of ten cases (front page: PyPI, vcpkg, npm, CocoaPods, Swift Package Index; documented public API: crates.io, Maven Central for both Java and Kotlin). Go is the single exception: its qualifying index publishes no headline total anywhere, verified by retrieving pkg.go.dev, pkg.go.dev/about, go.dev and a pkg.go.dev search page, so the count came from the other count_source the rule permits - the index's documented public API - as an exact enumeration of 139,128 distinct module paths, with no estimation or extrapolation. No language was scored from reputation. Checking the ten assignments together: the five languages at 100 all have a selected index above 100,000 by a factor of at least 1.39 (Go 139k, Swift 108k, Rust 336k, Maven Central 662k for Java and Kotlin, PyPI 896k, npm 2M+); the one language at 60 (C++, 2,862) is separated from them by more than an order of magnitude and from the 0s by three bands; the two languages at 0 both have zero qualifying indexes. No two languages with the same observable evidence received different levels: Java and Kotlin select the same index and receive the same level, and Zig and Quidra both have no qualifying index and receive the same level. No language received a level its band does not contain.
limitations: Evidence was accessed on 2026-09-18, one day after the frozen evidence cutoff of 2026-09-17. Package indexes grow monotonically, so every recorded count is at or slightly above its cutoff value. No language sits within 1% of a band boundary except Swift (CocoaPods at 'over 108 thousand' against a 100,000 boundary, an 8% margin, and a figure the index states as a floor), so no band assignment is sensitive to the one-day offset.

Swift is the one language whose level depends on which qualifying index is selected. CocoaPods (108k+) and the Swift Package Index (11,842) both qualify; the frozen rule selects the largest, giving 100. Under a narrower reading that counted only a Swift-exclusive index, Swift would be 80. The frozen document does not authorise that narrower reading and prohibits reinterpretation at scoring time, so 100 is recorded, with this sensitivity disclosed.

Go's count is a verified lower bound (139,128 distinct module paths from 272 windows of the index's documented public API), not the index's exact total, because no first-party total is published. The true total is higher; both figures fall in the same top band, so the level is unaffected. If a future run finds a published Go total, it should replace this figure.

ConanCenter's qualification for C++ could not be established or refuted exhaustively: the frozen C++ documentation roots were spot-checked at isocpp.org (home and get-started) rather than crawled in full, and clang.llvm.org, llvm.org/docs and developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode were not crawled for index references. This does not affect the level: ConanCenter's 1,948 recipes fall in the same 1,000-9,999 band as the selected index, vcpkg's 2,862.

Java's qualification rests on clause (ii) rather than clause (i): a crawl of 90 openjdk.org pages found no reference to Maven Central on openjdk.org itself, and the Oracle JDK documentation names Maven and Gradle rather than Maven Central by name. The chain Oracle-documentation-names-Maven plus Maven's-default-remote-is-Central is recorded with both excerpts.

Maven Central's numFound (661,801) counts distinct groupId:artifactId packages via the search.maven.org REST API; central.sonatype.com publishes no headline total on its front page. The API figure is the index operator's own published count.
npm's and CocoaPods' totals are published as floors ('more than two million packages', 'over 108 thousand libraries') rather than exact integers. Both floors determine the band unambiguously.

npmjs.com and swiftpackageindex.com are behind JavaScript/Cloudflare checks that block plain curl; their front-page figures were read with the built-in browser instead. The figures are the sites' own published counts either way.

No language was scored from a source type another language was not examined under: all ten were tested for a qualifying index under the same three clauses (E2) and for a self-published count (E4), including Quidra and Zig, for which the E4 record is the rubric-defined 'no qualifying index at the evidence cutoff'.
